Một task refactor lớn thường không hỏng ở dòng code đầu tiên. Nó hỏng vì lúc plan chưa nhìn đủ scope, đến lúc cook mới phát hiện migration, background job hoặc test bị bỏ sót.

--deep và --tdd giải quyết hai rủi ro khác nhau:

🔹 --deep là MODE — đổi pipeline planning, scout từng phase, có researcher + red-team + validation
🔹 --tdd là FLAG — compose được với mọi mode, ép viết test bảo vệ behavior cũ TRƯỚC khi refactor
🔹 Đi chung khi task vừa rộng vừa có behavior cũ cần giữ (ví dụ tách billing module: retry, idempotency, webhook replay, status transition)
🔹 KHÔNG dùng --deep cho task <5 file. KHÔNG dùng --tdd cho greenfield
🔹 /clear giữa plan và cook để giảm context nặng

Bài viết có decision matrix cho từng tình huống, template prompt chi tiết, pitfalls thường gặp (vd --tdd vô tình chụp test cho code có bug sẵn), và phần "Inside" mổ xẻ cơ chế researcher/red-team thực sự chạy thế nào.

Just shipped a writeup on /ck:plan --deep --tdd — when each is worth the cost, and when shorter modes are the better call.

Key distinction most folks miss:

• --deep is a MODE: changes the plan pipeline (researcher pass, per-phase scout, red-team, validation)
• --tdd is a FLAG: composes with any mode, forces tests-first ordering at both plan and cook time

They solve different risks:

→ Don't know enough scope yet → --deep gives you a file inventory + dependency map per phase
→ Worried refactor breaks running behavior → --tdd snapshots behavior with tests before code changes

Pair them for major refactors (e.g. splitting a billing module while keeping retry/idempotency/webhook contracts).

Don't pair for greenfield or <5-file tweaks — there's no behavior to snapshot, and the planning overhead doesn't pay off.

Full post covers decision matrix, prompt templates, and the gotcha where --tdd accidentally locks in pre-existing bugs as "current behavior."

linkedin.content:
I've been refining how I approach larger refactors with Claude Code, and one decision keeps coming up: when to use /ck:plan --deep --tdd, and when shorter modes are smarter.

The short version: they solve different risks.

--deep is a MODE that changes the planning pipeline. It runs 2-3 researcher passes for architecture analysis, scouts each phase individually (not just the overall scope), adds a red-team review, and forces a validation step. The output is a phase file with concrete file inventory, dependency maps, and test gap analysis — not just bullet points.

--tdd is a FLAG that composes with any mode. It restructures both the plan output and the cook execution order: tests get written FIRST to snapshot existing behavior, then refactor happens, then the regression gate (a specific compile/test command) must pass before moving on.

When to pair them:
• Major refactor (5+ areas, architectural debt)
• Code is running in production / has users
• Specific behavior must be preserved (retry logic, idempotency, API contracts, webhook handling)

Classic example: splitting a billing module out of a monolith. The scope spans API routes, database schema, background jobs, admin UI, and shared contracts. Behaviors like retry-then-fail-after-3, single-application-per-event-id, and refund-blocked-on-voided-invoice all need to survive.

When NOT to pair them:
• Small fixes (<5 files) — use --fast or default
• Greenfield code — there's no existing behavior to snapshot
• When the approach itself is unclear — use /ck:brainstorm first

The post also covers a subtle pitfall: --tdd can accidentally lock in pre-existing bugs as "current behavior" (e.g., duplicate webhooks creating duplicate payments). If the team is aware of known bugs, they should be declared in the task description, or split into a separate fix-then-refactor plan.

If you're using ClaudeKit on larger codebases, this writeup gives a concrete decision matrix, prompt templates, and an Inside section breaking down what --deep actually costs in tokens and time.
